Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.

New Delhi, 1 July 2026

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

text:
Why RMG can restart after the 10 Feb 2026 IT Rules amendment — and why it still hasn’t (yet). A legal breakdown:

The 10 Feb 2026 amendment to the IT Rules did not repeal or dilute the PROGA 2025 Act.
What it did was introduce a conditional statutory exception — not an automatic revival.

1️⃣ The baseline position: PROGA 2025's criminal prohibition

Under Section 5, PROGA 2025:
“No person shall offer, aid, abet, induce or otherwise engage in the offering of any online money game or online money gaming service.”

Violation attracts Section 9 penalties:

➡️ up to 3 years’ imprisonment and/or ₹1 crore fine.
This prohibition became effective from the date of Presidential assent (22 Aug 2025) — no rule-making required.

2️⃣ Why payments stopped — and why they matter:

Under Section 7, PROGA 2025:
“No bank, financial institution or payment intermediary shall engage in, permit, aid or facilitate any transaction towards payment for any online money gaming service.”
This made UPI, cards, wallets and gateways criminally exposed if they processed RMG transactions.
Hence the immediate, industry-wide payment freeze.

3️⃣ What the 10 Feb 2026 IT Rules amendment actually changed:

The amendment introduced the concept of a “permissible online real-money game” under the IT Rules framework.
Crucially, it says:

- A real-money game is not prohibited only if it is
• verified as permissible
• certified by a government-recognised Self-Regulatory Organisation (SRO)
• compliant with prescribed safeguards.
This is an exception clause — not a repeal.

4️⃣ How this legally unlocks PROGA (if conditions are met)
Once a game is certified as “permissible” under the IT Rules:

It falls outside the definition of a prohibited “online money game”
(A) Section 5 PROGA no longer applies to that game,
(B) Section 7 payment ban no longer triggers
(C) Advertising restrictions tied to “online money games” also lift for that specific certified game
(D) No certification = PROGA ban continues in full force.

5️⃣ Why RMG hasn’t restarted at scale despite the amendment:

Because, as of now:
- SRO recognition is limited / evolving
- Certification is game-specific, not platform-wide
- Any misclassification risks criminal prosecution, not just regulatory fines
- Platforms will not operate on “interpretation” when jail liability exists.

6️⃣ Most important legal shift (often missed):

Earlier:
Courts decided skill vs chance post-facto.
Now:
Statutory gatekeeping precedes operation.
No SRO approval → no legality → no payments.

7️⃣ Bottom line:

The Feb 10, 2026 amendment did not “revive” RMG.
It created a narrow, conditional doorway.

RMG can restart only game-by-game, only after SRO certification, and only within IT Rules safeguards.

Until then, PROGA’s criminal prohibitions remain fully operative.
Law changed — but risk calculus didn’t.

#PROGA2025 #OnlineGamingLaw #RMG #ITRules2026 #LegalAnalysis #GamingRegulationIndia

Hi Creators!

ASK ME QUESTIONS REGARDING X RULES ON POSTING YOUR CONTENT.

I WILL ANSWER THEN WITH PLEASURE.

Here’s one hypothetical question that intrigues every creator’s mind.

And the answer follows.

Q: Does X take it as violation of rules if posts created by AI or Grok are posted on the platform?

A: No. Posting content created by AI, including Grok, is not itself a violation of X’s rules.

X’s rules focus on deception, harm, spam, and certain restricted categories—not on whether a person or a model wrote or generated the post.

What the rules actually say:

Under the Authenticity policy, synthetic or manipulated media is restricted only when it is shared deceptively and is likely to cause harm (for example, widespread confusion on public issues, public-safety risk, or serious harm). 

That includes media of a real person fabricated or simulated with AI. Sharing the same kind of media in a non-deceptive way is allowed. X may also label synthetic media so people can see the context.
Ordinary AI-written text, images, or video—jokes, commentary, art, summaries, fictional scenes, and similar posts—does not violate the rules just because AI made them.

Narrower limits that do apply: 

•Creator Revenue Sharing (announced March 2026): unlabeled AI-generated videos of armed conflict can get a creator suspended from the revenue program for 90 days, and permanently on a repeat. That is a monetization penalty, not a general ban on AI posts.

•Spam and platform manipulation still apply. Bulk, duplicative, or automated posting that manipulates reach or trends can be enforced whether a human or an AI wrote it. Developer rules also require prior approval for AI-powered automated reply bots.

•Fake personas that use AI-generated profile photos or bios to deceive others are not allowed.

•AI-generated child sexual exploitation material is prohibited, as is non-consensual intimate imagery (including synthetic). Consensual adult AI content is allowed if it is labeled like other adult content.

•In India, under the IT Rules Amendment 2026, users must declare synthetically generated information that looks real and label it prominently. X says it watermarks images and videos generated or edited by Grok.

So a normal post drafted or illustrated by Grok is fine. Problems arise only if the post is spam, impersonation, unlabeled misleading media that can cause harm, or another existing rule violation.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 Condemns the Blocking of Bitchat in India

On 3 October 2026, @jack shared on @X a notice from @Apple App Review, which stated that Bitchat had been removed from the India App Store pursuant to a blocking order issued by @GoI_MeitY under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (“IT Act”). The notice further showed that Apple understood the order to mean that Bitchat ‘includes content that is illegal in India’, and on this basis cited a violation of Guideline 5 of its App Review Guidelines.

At present, the application is also reported to be unavailable on the @GooglePlay, and its official website is inaccessible on several Internet Service Providers.

What is Bitchat, and why does it matter?

Bitchat is a decentralised, peer-to-peer messaging app that works over Bluetooth mesh, with no internet or cellular connection, and no central server. Furthermore, it requires no mandatory user registration, and keeps messages secured with end-to-end encryption. Beyond privacy, its value is resilience, as it helps people communicate through the internet shutdowns that the government imposes during citizen protests. Bitchat’s popularity in India surged during the repeated, unconstitutional internet shutdowns imposed by the government around Jantar Mantar, New Delhi, at the time of the NEET UG protests in July 2026.

Blocked through an Unconstitutional Procedure

According to Apple’s App Review notice, Bitchat has been blocked under Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009 (“Blocking Rules 2009”). Jack Dorsey’s post on X suggests that the developers were neither heard nor served with a blocking order before the application was blocked. He learned of the block only through Apple’s notice, which is all he was able to share.

In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1 (paras 114 and 115), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the blocking procedure under Section 69A read with the Blocking Rules 2009, by heavily relying on the procedural safeguards built into this power, including, (1) recording of reasons in writing in the blocking order, which would be amenable to challenge in a writ petition, and (2) opportunity of hearing to the originator of the information before the order is passed under Rule 8. However, in consistent practice, the procedure under the Blocking Rules 2009 is applied in a manner that defeats these safeguards, rendering the blocking process under Section 69A and the Blocking Rules unconstitutional, as follows:

- By relying on the expression ‘person or intermediary’ in Rule 8, notice is invariably served only upon the intermediary and never upon the originator, even under normal circumstances. This practice egregiously deprives the originator of a fair opportunity to present their case against the request or complaint for blocking their information, thereby constituting a violation of the principles of natural justice, particularly audi alteram partem. This ultimately culminates in a situation where the originator’s fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) is curtailed without following a due and fair procedure in accordance with Article 14 of the Constitution of India.

- Furthermore, Rule 16 imposes an overarching requirement of confidentiality regarding requests and complaints for blocking information, as well as the actions taken thereon, including the final blocking order restricting public access to the information. This confidentiality provision enables the government agency to withhold, and simultaneously impedes the intermediary from providing, all relevant details to the affected person/originator of the information in a transparent manner.

- When combined with the practice followed under Rule 8, Rule 16 prevents the affected person from furnishing clarifications or a response to the blocking request, thereby depriving them of a fair opportunity to present their case. Furthermore, the affected person or originator is also deprived of a reasoned order blocking their information. This constitutes a clear violation of the principles of natural justice. Moreover, the above culminates in a situation where information is blocked under Section 69A of the IT Act, restricting the originator’s fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression, through a procedure that is manifestly arbitrary and devoid of procedural fairness.

The blocking of Bitchat is not an isolated instance. Over time, India has witnessed an increasing trend of opaque information blocking under Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules 2009, without any intimation to the affected person or originator, let alone furnishing them with the blocking order. These concerns were recently brought into sharp focus once again when @Cockroachisback's  X account was blocked without any transparency in May 2026.

Alarmed by this pattern and concerned about the violation of citizens’ digital and constitutional rights, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 filed a Public Interest Litigation in February 2025 before the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India, challenging, inter alia, the legality of Rules 8 and 16 of the Blocking Rules 2009, as violative of Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution of India. The case is titled ‘Software Freedom Law Center, India and Anr. v. Union of India and Anr.’, bearing W.P.(C) No. 161/2025, and is presently pending for further adjudication before the Supreme Court.

In the said Petition, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has sought that Rule 16 ought to be struck down as unconstitutional, being violative of Articles 14, 19(1)(a) and 21 of the Constitution of India. Furthermore, it has prayed that Rule 8 either be struck down as unconstitutional or be read down to interpret “or” as “and”, thereby mandatorily requiring the issuance of notice to the originator of information, ensuring conformity with the Constitution.

The illegal blocking of Bitchat

As of now, no blocking order is publicly available, and without it the specific grounds relied upon cannot be assailed. In any event, using Section 69A of the IT Act to block an entire application that enables communication is highly disproportionate.

Furthermore, the block immediately followed the internet shutdown imposed by the government on 2 October 2026 during a protest at Jantar Mantar. This timing gives rise to a strong inference that the application may have been targeted because it enables communication during internet shutdowns and protests. Enabling communication among protesters cannot, in any circumstance, be a valid ground for blocking an application under Article 19(2) or Section 69A.

Moreover, when the Delhi High Court upheld such exercise of power under Section 69A in ‘Telegram FZ LLC & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors.’, 2026:DHC:5145, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 noted that the judgment set a dangerous precedent. Interpreting “information” in Section 69A so expansively as to permit the blocking of an entire application can have far-reaching adverse consequences, particularly by allowing communication channels to be disabled during protests.

Without prejudice to https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s position that the decision sets a dangerous precedent, the Delhi High Court itself heavily relied on the temporary nature of the ban in reaching its conclusion. Here, the ban appears to be indefinite, which makes it all the more disproportionate and unconstitutional.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly urges the government to withdraw its orders directing Apple, Google and internet service providers to block the Bitchat application, as such orders are unconstitutional and violate citizens’ rights under Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 also calls upon Apple to firmly stand by the fundamental rights of its users in India. Apple should not give effect to the order mechanically, and should diligently take all appropriate steps, including legal remedies, to ensure that it does not become complicit in the violation of its users' fundamental rights.

Those Protesting Against NEET Paper Leak Make A Website Which Then Gets Compromised, Personal Details Of Volunteers Leaked : 
The Joke That Is CJP

The Cockroach Janta Party, founded by Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) member Abhijeet Dipke, has compromised the sensitive personal information of people who were misled into believing that he was fighting for the cause of ‘students’ in the aftermath of the NEET paper leak.

For the unversed, Dipke had called upon his followers to register on his party’s website :
https://t.co/KlVSTjKcp6
soon after it was launched.

Later, the AAP member alleged that the government took down his website, a claim that was later found to be false. It has now come to light that the users who trusted Abhijeet Dipke with their personal information have now been left vulnerable at the hands of potential cybercriminals.

On Wednesday (1st July), OSINT expert Nisarga took to X (formerly Twitter) to expose vulnerabilities on the website of the Cockroach Janta Party.

Earlier in its brief existence, the site was live and then responded with standard HTTP 403 errors from Hostinger’s active servers before the hold took effect.

In domain management terms, “clientHold” is a standard EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) status code controlled exclusively by the registrar, not by governments or external authorities. According to ICANN documentation and registrar policies, this status instructs the registry not to publish the domain in the DNS, effectively taking it offline until the registrar resolves the underlying issue. Such instruction can be issued only by the owner of the website, not third parties, not even governments. Alternately, the domain provider or the host can take the website offline due to various reasons.

It is commonly applied for routine administrative reasons such as incomplete WHOIS contact verification, billing or payment problems, compliance violations, or at the request of the domain owner. The clientHold affects resolution globally at the registry level, not at any country level.

On the other hand, when a government orders blocking a website, it is done through ISPs (Internet Service Providers) in the country, and the block only takes place in that country. In India, such a block is typically enforced through the Department of Telecommunications via ISP-level DNS poisoning, IP blacklisting, or URL filtering. Such actions allow the domain to still resolve correctly on international resolvers outside the country. That is why websites blocked by the Indian govt can be accessed in India through VPN.

Moreover, when one visits a website blocked by the govt, the browser displays a message saying the same. But when one visits cockroachjantaparty’s website, the browser displays the code DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN. This means the browser can’t find the domain because it has been deactivated.

Moreover, no public government orders, court directives, or official statements have been issued regarding https://t.co/n5u5L8JbZ5, further undermining the censorship claim.

Therefore, the analysis of the website shows that either it has been taken by Dipte himself, or the domain provider/host took it down due to some compliance issues. There is no evidence that the site was taken down on Indian government’s order.

One of the simplest ways for a government or large authority to restrict access to certain websites across a region is DNS-level blocking through ISP resolvers. In India, this is exactly how most website restrictions are enforced. By default, your device relies on the ISP’s DNS resolver, so DNS-based blocking takes effect automatically. However, this can often be bypassed by switching to third-party DNS resolvers such as Cloudflare(1.1.1.1) or Google (8.8.8.8).

Compared to this, China is much stricter, as China deploys censorship at multiple network layers simultaneously, making circumvention exponentially harder.

China’s Great Firewall works by checking internet traffic at many different levels, not just DNS. It uses Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) to look inside data packets as they travel through the network. It performs SNI inspection to read the domain name you’re trying to reach during the HTTPS handshake, which is why simply switching DNS doesn’t bypass it.

It also blocks the entire IP ranges of platforms like Google, Facebook, and YouTube at the router level, so even if you obtain the correct IP through a service like Cloudflare DNS, the connection is immediately dropped.

The system carries out active probing, where it tests servers that appear to be VPNs and blocks them quickly if confirmed. Finally, it uses protocol fingerprinting to study traffic patterns such as packet timing and size to detect VPN or proxy traffic even when the data is fully encrypted.

China is highly dedicated to preventing people from using foreign websites and instead pushes them to use their own.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

The Cockroach Janta Party, founded by Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) member Abhijeet Dipke, has compromised the sensitive personal information of people who were misled into believing that he was fighting for the cause of ‘students’ in the aftermath of the NEET paper leak.

For the unversed, Dipke had called upon his followers to register on his party’s website :
https://t.co/KlVSTjKcp6
soon after it was launched.

Later, the AAP member alleged that the government took down his website, a claim that was later found to be false. It has now come to light that the users who trusted Abhijeet Dipke with their personal information have now been left vulnerable at the hands of potential cybercriminals.

On Wednesday (1st July), OSINT expert Nisarga took to X (formerly Twitter) to expose vulnerabilities on the website of the Cockroach Janta Party.

Earlier in its brief existence, the site was live and then responded with standard HTTP 403 errors from Hostinger’s active servers before the hold took effect.

In domain management terms, “clientHold” is a standard EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) status code controlled exclusively by the registrar, not by governments or external authorities. According to ICANN documentation and registrar policies, this status instructs the registry not to publish the domain in the DNS, effectively taking it offline until the registrar resolves the underlying issue. Such instruction can be issued only by the owner of the website, not third parties, not even governments. Alternately, the domain provider or the host can take the website offline due to various reasons.

It is commonly applied for routine administrative reasons such as incomplete WHOIS contact verification, billing or payment problems, compliance violations, or at the request of the domain owner. The clientHold affects resolution globally at the registry level, not at any country level.

On the other hand, when a government orders blocking a website, it is done through ISPs (Internet Service Providers) in the country, and the block only takes place in that country. In India, such a block is typically enforced through the Department of Telecommunications via ISP-level DNS poisoning, IP blacklisting, or URL filtering. Such actions allow the domain to still resolve correctly on international resolvers outside the country. That is why websites blocked by the Indian govt can be accessed in India through VPN.

Moreover, when one visits a website blocked by the govt, the browser displays a message saying the same. But when one visits cockroachjantaparty’s website, the browser displays the code DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN. This means the browser can’t find the domain because it has been deactivated.

Moreover, no public government orders, court directives, or official statements have been issued regarding https://t.co/n5u5L8JbZ5, further undermining the censorship claim.

Therefore, the analysis of the website shows that either it has been taken by Dipte himself, or the domain provider/host took it down due to some compliance issues. There is no evidence that the site was taken down on Indian government’s order.

AN APOLOGY IS NO SUBSTITUTE FOR CONSTITUTIONAL COMPLIANCE: SUPREME COURT EXPOSES EXECUTIVE OVERREACH IN DELHI INTERNET BAN

The unfolding of this episode is a telling commentary on the precarious state of our constitutional governance. That the government, faced with the judicial scrutiny of an internet ban—a measure that strikes at the very root of the freedom of speech and expression guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a)—has chosen to tender an unconditional apology, is a tacit admission of executive overreach.
 
However, an apology, however unconditional, cannot act as a panacea for a constitutional transgression. It is deeply concerning that an order imposing a blanket internet shutdown in the capital—crippling the flow of information and stifling dissent—was passed, seemingly without the application of mind, only to be withdrawn or apologized for once the judicial microscope was applied.
 
The Supreme Court is not merely a forum for dispute resolution; it is the ultimate sentinel on the qui vive, the guardian of the citizen's liberties against the might of the State. While the unconditional apology is noted, the Court must not allow this hasty retreat to bury the larger, grave questions of proportionality and legality under the guise of commotion.

The issuance of notice in the connected matters is a welcome step. The majesty of the Constitution demands that the executive be held accountable, for the rule of law cannot be reduced to a mere game of catch-me-if-you-can, where the State breaches fundamental rights and then seeks to absolve itself through a written apology.

text:
🚨 Exposing a brand in India? 

Before you post, you need to know if they can actually get your video taken down for speaking your truth."

[Do Not Skip This Part]👇
Note: This tweet is only for general understanding of how this happens. A recent tracking down of a video involving the brand has occurred. Here is a thread to understand how it happens. Please refrain from mentioning the brand name or creator name in comments or replies to this tweet. 
 
In India, there is no simple rule allowing a brand to remove a video simply because it criticizes the brand. 

The usual route is a mix of:

IT Act + IT Rules + platform policy + civil court injunction/defamation/commercial disparagement suit.

1) What is the core legal structure?

Platforms like YouTube, X, Instagram, etc. are treated as intermediaries. They get “safe harbor” protection for user-generated content, but they may lose that protection if they ignore valid legal directions.

Under India’s intermediary framework, a platform gets legally strong “actual knowledge” mainly through:

A court order, or
A government/authorized agency direction/intimation

A private brand complaint alone usually does not automatically force a platform to remove a video. 

The Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India - clarified that platforms should not be forced to decide legality merely based on private complaints; the stronger trigger is a court order or government direction.

2) How does a brand complaint become a court order?

The structure usually works like this:

Step 1: The brand's legal team collects evidence

The company gathers the video URL, transcript, screenshots, claims made in the video, alleged false statements, impact on reputation, possible business loss, and proof of harm.

Step 2: The brand's legal team may send a legal notice

This is often the first pressure step. The brand may demand a takedown, an apology, a correction, damages, or the removal of specific claims.

Step 3: The brand files a civil/commercial suit.

If the creator does not comply, the brand can file a case for defamation, commercial disparagement, trademark issues, unfair trade practice, or reputational/business harm.

Step 4: The brand asks for urgent interim relief

The brand may request an interim injunction, sometimes ex parte, meaning the court can issue a temporary order without first hearing the creator if it believes urgent harm may occur.

Step 5: The court checks the matter prima facie

At this stage, the court is not finally deciding who is right. It checks whether there is an arguable case that the content may be false, misleading, malicious, defamatory, or commercially disparaging.

Step 6: The court may pass an injunction

The order can direct the creator to remove the video, stop sharing it, stop repeating certain claims, or restrain publication of similar allegedly disparaging content.

Step 7: The court order is sent to the platform
Once YouTube/X/Instagram receives the order, the platform may remove or disable access to the video to comply and protect its intermediary safe harbor.

3) Does the brand need to contact the platform grievance officer?

They can, but for defamation or brand-disparagement disputes, the platform may not want to act purely on the brand’s private complaint unless the violation is very clear under platform policy.

The more powerful route is:

Brand → Court → Court order → Platform compliance

The grievance officer becomes important when the platform receives a complaint, legal notice, or court/government order. But the grievance officer is not usually the final judge of whether a review is defamatory or fair criticism.

4) Can a video be removed just because it criticizes a company?

No. Criticism alone should not be enough.

A creator can usually criticize a product, company, service, pricing, quality, privacy policy, design, marketing claims, or consumer experience.

But risk increases when the video makes strong factual claims, such as:

“this phone is fake”
“this company is cheating customers”
“this is just a rebranded phone”
“do not buy this because the company is lying”
“this brand is a scam”

These claims need proof. If the creator presents them as facts and the company says they are false, misleading, malicious, or damaging to business, the company may go to court.

5) What does the court usually look at?

For a temporary injunction, the court may consider:

Prima facie case: Is there an arguable case that the content is false, misleading, defamatory, or commercially disparaging?

Balance of convenience: Who will suffer more harm if the order is or is not granted?

Irreparable harm: Can the damage to reputation or business be fixed later with money, or is immediate restraint needed?

Proof and testing: Did the creator rely on reliable documents, technical tests, expert analysis, official sources, or only assumptions?

Language used: Was the tone fair and analytical, or aggressive and conclusive without enough proof?

6) What can the creator do after an ex parte order?

The creator can challenge the order in the same court. 

They can ask the court to vacate or modify the injunction and argue that:
the video was fair comment,
the claims were based on evidence,
the company suppressed facts,
the order was passed without hearing the creator,
the takedown is too broad,
or public interest requires the video to remain available.

7) Practical creator lesson

A review video is safer when it clearly separates:

Opinion: “In my view, this looks like poor value.”

Fact: “The model number matches X device.”

Evidence: screenshots, teardown, software logs, official filings, import data, product pages, privacy policy, benchmark/test method.

Limitations: “Based on my testing,” “I could not independently verify X,” “the brand has been contacted for comment.”

The danger zone is when the creator makes a strong factual allegation without showing a reliable testing method or source.

Important point:
Fair criticism is not illegal. But factual claims like “fake phone”, “rebranded phone”, “scam”, “company is cheating” need strong proof.

Disclaimer: I have shared only how the law is applied in such cases; this tweet does not reflect my opinion or view on any similar incident. 

Bookmark this for the future; this will be useful for a lot of creators out there.

text:
मोदी जी द्वारा दिए गए कल डिजिटल मंचों और लोकतंत्र को लेकर अपने झूठे विचार रखे जिनकी पोल खुल चुकी है।
दिल्ली में पत्रकारों, यू ट्यूबर,सोशल मीडिया एक्टिविस्ट को पीटा गिरफ्तार किया गया, सोशल मीडिया एकाउंट बंद किए जा रहे है लगातार।

कंपनियां हर महीने भारत सरकार को अपनी 'मासिक अनुपालन रिपोर्ट' (Monthly Compliance Report) सौंपती हैं
Facebook और Instagram (Meta): मेटा ने भारत के अन्दर 6 महीनों में 1.6 लाख (160,000) से अधिक अकाउंट्स पर सीधे बड़ी कार्रवाई की है।
• ट्विटर (X एक्स: एक महीने की अवधि में ही भारत में 5 लाख से अधिक अकाउंट्स को पूरी तरह बैन किया है। जिनमें कुछ समाचार पोर्टल और पत्रकारों के हैंडल भी शामिल थे।

गृह मंत्रालय के 'सहयोग पोर्टल' (Sahyog Portal) और IT एक्ट की धाराओं के तहत मार्च से जुलाई 2026 के बीच करीब 1.95 लाख (195,000) कंटेंट ब्लॉकिंग और टेकडाउन आदेश जारी किए गए। यह औसतन हर 68 सेकंड में एक आदेश के बराबर है।
• Instagram: सबसे ज़्यादा लगभग 1 लाख (100,000) ब्लॉकिंग आदेश मिले।
• Facebook: करीब 80,000 टेकडाउन और ब्लॉकिंग निर्देश दिए गए。
• YouTube: लगभग 15,000 आदेश जारी किए गए।

प्रधानमंत्री नरेंद्र मोदी ने नई दिल्ली में आयोजित आठवें ब्लूमबर्ग न्यू इकोनॉमी फोरम (Bloomberg New Economy Forum) में देश के डिजिटल मंचों और लोकतंत्र को लेकर अपने विचार रखे।
उन्होंने भारत को 'लोकतंत्र की जननी' (Mother of Democracy) बताया और कहा कि भारत में 100 से अधिक भाषाएं, करीब 80,000 पंजीकृत समाचार पत्र और 1,000 से ज्यादा सैटेलाइट टीवी चैनल मौजूद हैं।
उन्होंने बताया कि भारत में 50 करोड़ से अधिक लोग यूट्यूब और 50 करोड़ से अधिक लोग इंस्टाग्राम का इस्तेमाल करते हैं, जो ऑनलाइन नागरिक चर्चाओं में सक्रिय रूप से भाग लेते हैं।
उन्होंने कहा कि इन डिजिटल मंचों ने एक ऐसा मंच तैयार किया है जहां नागरिक खुले तौर पर विचारों का आदान-प्रदान और राष्ट्रीय मुद्दों पर बहस करते हैं।

text:
A Hyderabad founder spent four months building a B2B SaaS product. CRM integrations, three pricing tiers, onboarding that actually worked.

Two weeks before launch his co-founder asked what the cookie banner said.

There was no cookie banner. There were two documents, and neither of them had been written for this product.

The Terms of Service came from a competitor’s site. The Privacy Policy came from a template generator. Both had been pasted in during week one and never opened again.

He reached out to us with fourteen days on the clock. He was not asking for a document set. He wanted to know whether what he already had would survive contact with a paying customer.

So we read both documents against the product, not against each other.

The Privacy Policy said the platform collects name, email, and company name. That was true as far as it went.

It said nothing about the session replay tool running on every page, recording mouse movement and clicks from every visitor. 

Nothing about the analytics platform receiving behaviour data on export. 

Nothing about the CRM integration pulling contact records out of the customer’s own account.

Three tools were processing user data and a user reading the policy would never know they existed.

Under the DPDP Act, 2023 and the Rules notified on 13 November 2025, the notice has to itemize what is collected, the purpose, the retention, and who it is shared with. 

A policy that names three fields and omits three processors is not a short policy. It is an inaccurate one.

Then the liability cap. The template had a blank where the number goes and nobody had filled it in, so the contract capped his liability at zero.

Founders hear that and assume it is maximum protection. It is the opposite. 

A limitation clause that strips out all liability is the one most likely to be read against the drafter, and under UK law an unreasonable exclusion can be struck down entirely, which leaves the liability uncapped. 

The clause meant to protect him was the one most likely to disappear in a dispute.

The acceptable use clause prohibited uploading anything illegal. It said nothing about who owns uploaded data, whether the platform could use it to improve the product, or what happens to it when a subscription ends.

This is B2B. Every upload was a business customer’s data, which usually means it was someone else’s customer data two steps down the chain. Silence in the Terms is not a neutral position on that. If anything in the stack learns from customer data, silence means it is happening without a license.

The part I keep seeing is the sequence. 

Founders treat legal documents as a launch-day chore, something to generate the night before, when they are actually a product specification written in another language. 

The documents describe what the software does. If nobody checks them against what the software does, they describe a different product.

What I found harder to watch here was how well everything else had been built. 

Four months of careful work, and the one artefact he had outsourced to a template site was the first thing an enterprise buyer would open.

Here is what we did in the fourteen days.

We mapped every tool with access to user data, including the ones installed by his developer and never documented anywhere.

We rewrote the privacy notice to cover all of them, with purpose, retention, and third-party sharing set out against each.

We put a defensible number in the liability cap and rebuilt the clause around it.

We drafted the data ownership, permitted use, and model training position, plus deletion and export on termination.

We added the IT Rules disclosures, legal entity details and a named grievance officer, to the footer and the Terms.

The product launched three weeks later with a complete set. One week after that, the first enterprise prospect asked for a security and compliance review before signing. He had answers.

The comparison is not close. Two weeks of drafting before launch, against a DPDP penalty regime that runs up to ₹250 crore for security safeguard failures, and against the thing that actually kills early deals, which is a procurement team deciding you are too much work to onboard.

So here are three things to check before your next customer invite goes out.

Open your Privacy Policy and list every tool on your site that touches user data. Analytics, session replay, chat widget, CRM, email platform. If an SDK is installed and not named, your notice is wrong. Naming the obvious ones and skipping the rest is not a shorter policy.

Find the number in your liability cap. If the clause is blank, inherited, or set to zero, that is not conservative drafting. It is the clause your buyer’s counsel will spend the most time on.

Read what your Terms say about uploaded data. Ownership, permitted use, what happens on termination, and whether anything in your stack improves on it. If the document is silent on all four, you are relying on an assumption you never wrote down.

Two dates are now fixed. The Consent Manager framework switches on 13 November 2026. The obligations on notice, consent, security, and data principal rights apply from 13 May 2027.

Most founders who send us their documents believe the legal side is handled because the pages exist. 

The pages existing and the pages matching the product are different things, and the buyer’s counsel is the one who checks.

text:
This video is said to be from 2009. Look at how the Election Commission of India functioned then, and compare it with what is happening today.

The Election Commission freely encouraged citizens to exercise their voting rights. Its advertisements highlighted the problems people faced in everyday life, including corruption, poor education, inadequate healthcare, crumbling infrastructure and bad governance, and reminded them that the power to change these conditions lay in their votes.

The central purpose was to promote universal adult franchise, encourage electoral participation and increase voter turnout.

Watch this advertisement carefully. It clearly conveys the message that if the government has failed to deliver good governance, the citizens have the power to change it through elections.

Did anyone accuse the Election Commission of being biased or campaigning against the government? Did the government have to rush to its defence? Or was the Election Commission simply exercising its constitutional independence?

In 2013, following the Supreme Court’s intervention, VVPAT was introduced to strengthen transparency and build confidence among voters and political parties. The Supreme Court recognised that an independently verifiable paper trail was indispensable to free and fair elections.

Now look at what is happening.

When questions were raised about the extraordinary increase in reported voter turnout after 5 PM, political parties and citizens sought access to CCTV footage and election records.

The Punjab and Haryana High Court directed the Election Commission to provide the relevant footage and records. What followed?

Instead of making election records more accessible, the Central Government amended Rule 93 of the Conduct of Election Rules in December 2024, on the Election Commission’s recommendation, restricting public access to CCTV footage and other electronic election records.

Subsequently, the Election Commission introduced instructions permitting the destruction of CCTV footage and other recordings after just 45 days where no election petition had been filed.

Why should evidence relating to the conduct of elections be made inaccessible and then destroyed when transparency is precisely what establishes public confidence?

The Supreme Court rejected the demand for 100% VVPAT verification in 2024. But what is the purpose of an independently verifiable paper trail if its comprehensive verification is resisted? The very purpose of introducing VVPAT was to strengthen public confidence in election results.

And now we are witnessing something even more disturbing.

Instead of concentrating on enrolling every eligible citizen, the electoral roll revision has resulted in the removal of approximately 13 crore names. Genuine voters are being forced to struggle to establish their eligibility and recover their voting rights.

With an adult population exceeding 100 crore, the Election Commission must explain how many eligible citizens remain outside the electoral rolls and how many have been wrongly excluded.

The Election Commission’s constitutional responsibility is to ensure that every eligible citizen can vote, not to make citizens struggle to protect their existing voting rights.

Look at the complete reversal.

Earlier, the Election Commission encouraged citizens to vote, expanded participation and introduced measures to strengthen public confidence.

#ElectionCommissionOfIndia

Keralam makes history.

For the first time, the Keralam Legislative Assembly has passed a resolution seeking the removal of the Chief Election Commissioner.

The integrity of our electoral process is non-negotiable. Serious concerns over voter roll revisions, the disenfranchisement of eligible voters, and the impartiality of the Election Commission cannot be ignored.

Through this historic resolution, Keralam has put forward three clear demands:

1. Restore voting rights: Address the irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process and immediately restore the voting rights of all eligible voters who have been wrongfully excluded.

2. Remove the Chief Election Commissioner: Initiate proceedings to remove the Chief Election Commissioner, whose impartiality has come under serious question.

3. Reform the selection process: Reconstitute the Election Commissioners’ selection committee to include the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, and the Chief Justice of India, ensuring the independence and credibility of the institution.

The right to vote is the foundation of our democracy. No institution can be allowed to undermine the constitutional rights of our citizens.

Our stand is unequivocal. The right to vote must be protected. The Constitution must be upheld. Democracy must prevail.

Keralam stands firmly for free and fair elections.

#VDSatheesan #Keralam

Listening to the BJP's press conference today defending the Election Commission and dismissing the Opposition's protests and Rahul Gandhi's questions as "political drama." Their primary defence? "Congress gave party tickets to former CECs and made them Governors or Ministers; we haven't given a single political post to any Election Commissioner."

On the surface, that sounds like a clever rebuttal. What Congress did in the past—whether fielding T.N. Seshan on a party ticket or bringing M.S. Gill into the Rajya Sabha and making him a Union Minister—was institutionally indefensible.

But if the BJP genuinely wants to claim the moral high ground on the Election Commission's independence, hiding behind 20-year-old Congress precedents isn't enough. It needs to answer four fundamental questions:

1. Modern patronage doesn't always require a Raj BhavanYou claim no former CEC was rewarded with a government post. Technically true. But how does a former CEC like Rajiv Kumar walk into the boardroom of HDFC Bank as an Independent Director and Part-Time Chairman after retirement?  Yes, HDFC is a private bank—but anyone who understands India's financial sector knows that no top banking board or chairmanship appointment goes through without the explicit regulatory nod of the RBI, and by extension, the comfort of the Finance Ministry. In the 2020s, post-retirement rewards don't need to look like 1990s political tickets; regulatory-approved corporate boardrooms serve the exact same purpose with much cleaner optics.

2. If your intentions are clean, why didn't you ban post-retirement jobs in the 2023 Act? When this government passed the CEC and Other Election Commissioners Act in 2023, it had a historic opportunity to permanently shut the door that Congress used to exploit. Under our Constitution, the UPSC Chairman (Article 319) and the CAG (Article 148) are strictly barred from taking post-retirement government appointments. Every major electoral reform committee has demanded a strict cooling-off period and a post-retirement ban for Election Commissioners too. Why did the BJP deliberately leave that loophole wide open in the 2023 law? Was it an innocent oversight, or did you consciously keep that carrot alive for future use?

3. Why deny the other two Election Commissioners equal constitutional protection? Even today, while the Chief Election Commissioner can only be removed through a Parliamentary process similar to a Supreme Court judge, the other two Election Commissioners do not enjoy the same shield—they can still be removed on the recommendation of the CEC. When you rewrote the law from scratch in 2023, why didn't you grant the other two ECs the exact same security of tenure as the CEC so they could dissent without fear?

4. Why remove the Chief Justice of India from the selection panel? In March 2023, the Supreme Court tried to insulate the Election Commission from executive control by creating a balanced selection panel: the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition, and the CJI. Within months, the government brought the 2023 Act, removed the CJI, and replaced him with a Union Cabinet Minister—handing the ruling party a built-in 2:1 majority to handpick every Election Commissioner. If you want an independent umpire, why were you uncomfortable having the Chief Justice in the room?

Pointing at Congress's past sins is an easy TV debate tactic, not an institutional defence.

In a functional democracy, the referee doesn't just have to be neutral; the law must be structured so the referee cannot be compromised. When you give yourself a 2:1 majority to appoint the Commissioners, refuse to give the two ECs equal removal protection, and deliberately refuse to ban post-retirement plums by law—you forfeit the right to call it "drama" when citizens question the umpire.

Elon Musk vs Ambani: What is really happening with Starlink in India?

Elon Musk has now directly targeted Mukesh Ambani, sarcastically calling him the “real boss of India” over Starlink's delayed launch.

But here is the bigger picture.

India has already granted satellite communication licences to three players:

• Starlink — Elon Musk
• Jio Satellite Communications — Reliance
• Eutelsat OneWeb — backed by Bharti Enterprises, Airtel's parent group

All three are at broadly the same regulatory stage, according to the government.

The pending steps include security clearances and spectrum allocation.

So, is Starlink being blocked to protect Jio and Airtel?

There is no publicly established proof of that allegation. The government says the process is fair and non-discriminatory.

But one thing is clear: this is not just a fight between Elon Musk and Mukesh Ambani. It is about competition, regulation and who gets to serve India's next billion internet users.

The real question is simple: Should satellite internet providers be allowed to compete on equal terms, with the same rules for everyone?

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

The Neha Singh Rathore Controversy and the Constitutional Price of Reckless Journalism

The freedom of the press is a constitutional guarantee, not a licence to assassinate reputation.

ABP News has publicly apologised for a factually incorrect digital report concerning folk singer Neha Singh Rathore. The controversy raises a question larger than the reputation of one individual: what responsibility does a powerful media institution bear when its publication associates an identifiable woman with a profoundly stigmatising allegation?

The Constitution protects the freedom to report. It does not exempt a publisher from the consequences of unlawful defamation.

Article 19(1)(a) is the lifeblood of a free press. But Article 21 protects personal dignity and reputation, while Article 19(2) expressly recognises defamation as a permissible ground for reasonable restriction.

A free press is indispensable to democracy. An unaccountable press is not its constitutional ideal.

A correction may acknowledge the error. An apology may express regret. Neither necessarily restores the reputation of a person whose name or image has already been circulated in connection with an unfounded allegation.

The law must nevertheless distinguish negligence from deliberate falsehood. Liability cannot be determined by public outrage; it must be determined by evidence.

If the original publication conveyed a defamatory falsehood, the injured person is entitled to pursue the remedies that the law provides. The broadcaster is equally entitled to answer the allegation and explain the circumstances of its error.

The right to criticise a woman is protected. The right unlawfully to defame her is not.

There is no greater betrayal of journalistic responsibility than treating verification as optional and reputation as expendable.

The proper question is not merely whether the broadcaster has said sorry.

It is whether the truth has been restored, the injury adequately addressed and the professional failure subjected to independent scrutiny.

A FALSEHOOD CAN TRAVEL TO MILLIONS. AN APOLOGY MAY NEVER REACH THEM.

THE PRESS MUST BE FREE TO QUESTION POWER — AND ACCOUNTABLE WHEN IT WRONGFULLY INJURES THE POWERLESS.

— NK Goswami
Advocate, Supreme Court of India
